pamphlet_excerpts: Cut Protection: Carving gloves woven with Kevlar or stainless steel mesh protect the holding hand.
Blood Circle: Maintain a clear arm length boundary in every direction before opening any blade.
Wound Cleaning: Wash minor carving lacerations thoroughly with mild soap and potable clean running water.
Splinter Removal: Disinfect tweezers with isopropyl alcohol before gently extracting wood fragments along entry angles.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Glove Fitting: Don a snug cut resistant glove on the hand holding the wooden block.
Step 2 - Space Clearance: Establish a complete blood circle by extending both arms outwards in full rotation.
Step 3 - Direct Pressure: Press sterile gauze firmly over minor lacerations until bleeding halts completely without oozing.
Step 4 - Sterile Dressing: Cover the cleaned wound with antiseptic ointment and an adhesive sterile fabric bandage.

options: A. A dull blade slices through wood grain effortlessly, whereas a sharp blade requires you to push with your full body weight.
B. A sharp blade lets you carve directly toward your bare thumb without wearing any protective gear.
C. A sharp blade makes clean, controlled cuts with light pressure.

choices: A. A dull blade slices through wood grain effortlessly, whereas a sharp blade requires you to push with your full body weight.

misconception_pool.misconception: A dull carving knife is safer for beginners because the rounded edge cannot slice skin easily.
misconception_pool.fact: Dull blades require excessive force and slip off wood fibers unpredictably, causing deeper lacerations than sharp tools.

misconception_pool.misconception: Pulling a deep wood splinter out against the entry angle extracts the fragment faster.
misconception_pool.fact: Pulling against the entry angle breaks the wood fibers beneath the skin; always withdraw splinters along their entry path.

misconception_pool.misconception: Hydrogen peroxide should be poured into every fresh carving cut to sterilize the wound.
misconception_pool.fact: Hydrogen peroxide damages healthy healing tissue; flush minor cuts with clean running water and mild soap before bandaging.

misconception_pool.misconception: Peeking under a blood-soaked gauze pad every minute verifies whether bleeding has stopped.
misconception_pool.fact: Lifting a dressing disrupts forming clots and restarts bleeding; press fresh gauze directly on top of the soaked pad.

misconception_pool.misconception: A locking pocketknife makes it safe to push or pry with the spine and tip of the blade.
misconception_pool.fact: Blade locks can fail under sideways twisting or prying forces, so pressure must always keep the blade opening against the stop.

misconception_pool.misconception: Passing an open fixed-blade carving knife handle-first with the edge facing down is enough.

misconception_pool.misconception: Wearing a heavy leather glove on the knife-holding hand prevents accidental blade slips.
misconception_pool.fact: A cut-resistant thumb guard belongs on the holding hand, while the carving hand needs direct grip sensitivity on the handle.

misconception_pool.misconception: Setting unsheathed gouges loose in a tool roll protects their bevels between carving sessions.
misconception_pool.fact: Loose blades strike each other and nick their cutting edges; each gouge requires an individual edge guard or separate pocket.
